newsitem.title: USA: Camdessus says not nervous over forex markets.
newsitem.headline: Camdessus says not nervous over forex markets.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Michel Camdessus said on Thursday he saw no reason to be nervous about foreign exchange markets and current exchange rates had served the world well.
"I am not exceedingly nervous about foreign exchange markets at the moment," he said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

"We had during the last two years a welcome correction of a very adverse development in the markets. This correction has produced a new constellation of exchange rates which has served the world well," he said.
The current level of the yen "is justified at the present moment" but would not be justified in the medium term if the economy were to strengthen further, he said.
Camdessus welcomed the recent increase in U.S. interest rates by the Federal Reserve and thought market expectations for a further increase were deserved.
"It (the increase) has been implemented in an extremely prudent way, allowing the markets to be prepared and not to be taken by surprise," the IMF chief said.

"If I see what the forward markets tell us, it's clear that they expect some further tightening to take place sometime down the road during the year and I would be surprised if in this occurrence the markets were wrong."

"The consensus will be to allow exchange rates to change in line with cyclical upturns. I see such a consensus among key players," Camdessus, speaking ahead of a meeting of the Group of Seven finance ministers and central bankers on Sunday, said.
Asked about prospects for central bank intervention on foreign exchange markets, he said, "I don't see intervention by monetary authorities to be the first order of priority."
The first priority was for consolidation of economic policies, he said, adding that he saw no need for a rise in Japanese interest rates.
"I believe a continuation of the very accommodative monetary policies is well justified," he said.
He said Japan needed to consolidate its fiscal position, "which is worrying indeed and could not be sustainable in the medium-term perspective."
This needed to be done with caution, however. "Some flexibility would be in order for the Japanese authorities if they were to discover the recovery is faltering," he said.

He said he believed Europe should push ahead with plans to launch a single currency in 1999 and said he believed that parliamentary elections in Britain and France should strengthen the momemtum to monetary union.

He said that European Commission and International Monetary Fund forecasts on how close countries were to economic convergence criteria in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union appeared to him very similar.
"I am more impressed by the convergence of views between the EU and the IMF than the divergence," he said.

"Even if we are a little bit more on the downside than they are, you know in this kind of thing there is a broad margin of error. You are not in a kind of scientific, precise domain. I would not quarrel with half a point more or less."
He urged countries to continue budget consolidation. "It would be a mistake now to stop this effort after accomplishing so much, and indeed to start acting more decisively."
Asked what he thought about delaying EMU, he said, "I would suggest to go ahead and don't take the risk of the uncertainty ... any delay would create."
He said welcomed France's decision to hold an early two-round parliamentary election in May and June as potentially strengthening momentum to EMU.
"Elections are an essential element of democratic life. They are always a good thing. I do not see a negative factor in this domain.

"Governments will come back with a new mandate from the people, they will have a wonderful opportunity to explain to the people what is at stake, I think and I hope that if anything these elections in the two countries (France and Britain) could strengthen the momentum toward EMU."
